questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
Let $u=\frac{1}{x}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{sec}^{2}⁡(1/x)}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{1}{x})\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡u\cdot (-\text{d}u) \\  & =-\int {sec}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{1}{x})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Quotients Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

So, let $u=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $-1$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)$ | $1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)}^{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)}^{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1))-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1))\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Products Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{3}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =4\int {sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\int {sec}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{3})+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments
questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u=x-\frac{\pi }{4},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi /4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\pi /4$ | $0$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}3{sec}^{2}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}{sec}^{2}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{tan}⁡(u){|}_{-\pi /4}^{0} \\  & =3(0-(-1)) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments
questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u=x-\frac{\pi }{6},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /3$ | $2\pi /3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\pi /6$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}4\operatorname{csc}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{cot}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{csc}⁡(u)\operatorname{cot}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =4{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{csc}⁡(u)\operatorname{cot}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =-4\operatorname{csc}⁡(u){|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-4(\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})) \\  & =-4(1-2) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$
